analysis.investment_thesis: Ashapura Minechem fails both Magic Formula screens — earnings yield of ~5.4% is below the 6% threshold and ROIC of ~15% is below the 20% hurdle, meaning you're paying a fair-to-full price for a mediocre-return business. Chronically negative free cash flow (-₹208 Cr in FY25 despite ₹377 Cr EBIT) reveals a capital-hungry operation where reported earnings are not translating into real cash for shareholders.
key_strengths: Recovering revenue trajectory: ₹334 Cr (2020) → ₹2,739 Cr (2025), with EBITDA expanding strongly to ₹469 Cr
Diversified mineral portfolio (bauxite, bentonite, kaolin, proppants) across industrial, oil & gas, and specialty chemicals end-markets
ROE of 27.1% looks optically attractive, boosted by recent profitability recovery from deeply negative 2017–2020 period
key_risks: Persistently negative FCF for 5 straight years (-₹208 Cr in FY25); capex of ₹401 Cr consumed 85% of EBITDA — earnings yield is illusory without cash conversion
Debt nearly tripling: borrowings ₹441 Cr (2020) → ₹1,228 Cr (2025); finance costs CAGR 17.8% — debt-funded growth compresses true returns on capital
Severe historical cyclicality: revenue cratered 81% (2016→2020), operating income went deeply negative (-₹45 Cr in 2020); business is commodity-price and volume dependent
red_flags: Earnings Yield (EBIT/EV) = ₹377 Cr / ₹6,951 Cr EV ≈ 5.4% — below the Magic Formula's 6% minimum; stock is NOT cheap
FCF negative every single year shown (2020–2025); cumulative FCF burn ~-₹574 Cr while reporting net profits
Net profit in 2020 (₹383 Cr) was entirely driven by ₹487 Cr 'Other Income' vs. -₹45 Cr operating loss — earnings quality is poor
Revenue 9Y CAGR only 4.9% — essentially flat in real terms over a decade; no durable growth engine visible
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Magic Formula math is straightforward here and unfavorable on both legs. Earnings Yield: EBIT of ₹377 Cr divided by Enterprise Value (₹5,897 Cr market cap + ₹1,054 Cr net debt = ₹6,951 Cr EV) yields just 5.4% — below the 6% minimum that makes a stock "cheap" by this framework. Return on Capital: EBIT / Invested Capital (equity ₹1,426 Cr + debt ₹1,163 Cr - cash ₹109 Cr = ₹2,480 Cr) = ~15.2%, which is mediocre — the business is not generating the 20%+ returns that signal a true competitive moat. ROCE of 18.6% (company-reported) is at best adequate, not excellent.

The deeper problem is cash conversion. The ₹377 Cr EBIT evaporates when you look at cash flows: capex of ₹401 Cr in FY25 alone exceeds operating income, and FCF has been negative in every visible year. The company is funding growth with debt (borrowings up ₹787 Cr in 5 years) while finance costs compound at 17.8% CAGR. This is exactly the capital trap the Magic Formula is designed to avoid — a business that looks profitable on an income statement but destroys capital through relentless reinvestment with subpar returns. The 2017–2020 collapse (revenue down 81%, operating losses) shows this is a cyclical miner, not a compounder.
